Sample text:
---
# On Keeping Things That Don't Work

Every household has a drawer like this one. Mine is the second drawer in the kitchen, underneath the one with the takeout menus and the rubber bands that have fused into a single brittle lump. It holds cables. There are phone chargers for phones I no longer own, a mini-USB cord from a camera that went into a landfill years ago, two cables that might be for a printer, and a short white wire with a connector shaped like nothing I can identify. Some of them still work. I have never once been able to tell which ones, because I have never once tested them. I just open the drawer, look at the tangle, and close it again.

I want to think about that drawer, and about the larger category of things it represents: objects we keep not because they serve us but because they still mean something, or because throwing them away feels like a small betrayal we are not ready to commit. Dead batteries in the junk tray. A fountain pen with dried ink. A radio that hums but does not pick up stations. A wristwatch stopped at 4:17, which may have been the moment its battery gave out or may simply be the time someone once set it to and never corrected it.

It is worth asking why we do this. The easy answer is sentiment, and sentiment is part of it, but sentiment is too vague to explain much. The watch stopped at 4:17 is not sentimental in any obvious way. I did not inherit it from anyone famous. It belonged to a man I knew slightly, who wore it to a job he did for forty years and then gave it to me in a box with a card that said nothing useful. The watch does not tell time. It has not told time since before I got it. And yet I cannot quite make myself put it in the bin, and when I think about why, I arrive at something more interesting than sentiment. I arrive at the question of what an object is for once its function has gone.

Philosophers have a version of this puzzle in the old thought experiment of the Ship of Theseus. A ship is preserved by replacing its planks one at a time, until eventually none of the original wood remains. Is it the same ship? And if someone collected all the discarded planks and reassembled them into a second ship, which one would be the real Theseus? Most people feel the answer depends on something other than the materials. We track identity through history, through continuity of story and use, not through the atoms. The watch is a useful case because it has lost the one thing that made it a watch. Its gears are intact. Its hands are where they were. What has gone is its purpose, and so what remains is only its shape and its history. We keep it because it still has a past, even if it no longer has a future.

This is also why the cable drawer feels different from the watch. The cables are not mourned. They are simply deferred. Each one represents a possibility: that I might need this one day, that the old phone might be useful for a project, that I will someday sort the drawer on a rainy afternoon and feel virtuous. Keeping them is a small bet against my future laziness. I have lost that bet many times. The drawer is a monument to the gap between intention and follow-through, and, I suspect, to the way most of us keep more than we will ever use because letting go requires a decision, and a decision requires a certainty that we are rarely comfortable having.

There is a Japanese practice called kintsugi, in which broken pottery is mended with lacquer mixed with powdered gold or silver. The cracks are not hidden. They are highlighted, so that the repaired bowl shows its breaks as its most distinctive feature. The philosophy behind it is often described as an acceptance of impermanence and imperfection, and I find it a useful counterpoint to my drawer. Kintsugi does not pretend the object was never broken, and it does not pretend the broken object is worthless. It asks that the history of the damage be visible and even beautiful. My stopped watch is a kind of kintsugi bowl, I think, except that nobody has repaired it. It is simply broken and kept, which is a more honest and less dignified state.

But I am not sure the comparison holds, because kintsugi is an act of care that restores something, and my drawer is mostly an act of avoidance. There is a difference between keeping a thing because you have honored its story and keeping it because you cannot face the small labor of deciding what it is now. The watch sits in a box on a shelf, and I have never tried to repair it, which means I have never really decided whether it is a object worth fixing or a memento worth preserving exactly as it is. The stopped hands have made that decision for me, and I have allowed it because the alternative requires me to think about a man I did not know well and whether I did right by his gift.

Perhaps this is the real function of objects that no longer work. They are placeholders for relationships, for moments, for versions of ourselves that we are not quite finished with. The old camera reminds me of a summer I cannot fully recall but know was good, because I took photographs of it. The fountain pen belonged to a teacher who wrote comments in green ink on every essay I handed in, and although the pen no longer writes, its presence is a kind of permission to remember that I was once someone who wrote essays by hand and was occasionally praised for it. These objects work on us differently from functioning things. A working tool is absorbed into its use and forgotten. A broken one stays in view and keeps asking questions.

The economics of this are interesting too. Modern life has trained us to replace rather than repair. Devices are designed with batteries that cannot be swapped and screws that require special tools, and by the time something fails, a new version is already on sale, slightly thinner and faster, promising to make us forget the old one. In that environment, keeping a dead object is almost a quiet form of resistance. It says that the thing had value beyond its utility and that its value has not expired merely because its function has. Repair cafés have sprung up in many cities, where volunteers help people fix toasters, lamps, and bicycles. Their popularity suggests that many people feel the same unease I do about the throwaway habits of the age, and want some alternative, even if they are not sure what it looks like.

Still, I do not want to romanticize the drawer. Some of what I keep is simply clutter, and clutter has real costs. It takes up room, it makes the kitchen harder to use, and it can become a kind of low-level guilt, a reminder of intentions unfulfilled. Tidying books sometimes advise asking whether an object sparks joy, and while that formulation is cheerful to the point of absurdity, it points at something true. The question is not whether a thing is useful but whether keeping it is a living choice or a habit of not choosing. A cable I have not used in a decade is probably not worth the drawer space. The watch, I think, passes the test, though I would like to know more firmly why.

Maybe that is the point. Each object we keep is a small argument about what we value, and most of those arguments are never made explicitly. We simply find ourselves with drawers full of answers we did not consciously give. Taking inventory of them, as I have been doing here, is a way of making the arguments visible. Some I will win and keep the thing. Some I will lose and let it go. Either outcome is better than the vague pile that accumulates when we never look.

There is also something to be said for the humility of broken things. A stopped clock is right twice a day, the old saying goes, and a dead battery is a reminder that everything runs down eventually, including us. We are, in a sense, objects that no longer work as efficiently as we once did, and we are kept anyway, by the people who remember what we were for. Nobody throws away a grandmother because her hands shake now. We find other uses for her, or we simply keep her, because her worth was never only in her function. It would be strange, and a little cruel, to apply a different standard to the things we surround ourselves with.

So the drawer stays closed for now. I will probably open it again next month, look at the tangle, and close it again. The watch will keep sitting at 4:17, which may or may not be the moment it stopped, and I will continue not knowing whether to fix it or leave it as it is. I have come to think that this uncertainty is not a failure of nerve. It is simply what it feels like to live among objects that carry more than they can do. We are allowed to keep some things without a reason we can fully articulate. We are also allowed, eventually, to let some go. The skill, if there is one, lies in noticing which is which, and in admitting that the broken things often tell us more about ourselves than the working ones ever could.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. This is a reflective personal essay whose recurring objects and unresolved feelings give it a distinctive, intimate voice.

## Grounded reading
The voice is measured and self-questioning, moving from a familiar kitchen drawer toward larger questions of memory, identity, and worth. Its pathos gathers around the stopped watch and the man who gave it: the narrator is unsure whether keeping it honors a relationship or avoids deciding what to do with the gift. The essay invites the reader to inspect their own possessions without demanding either sentimental preservation or ruthless decluttering; its closing emphasis is on noticing and making a choice, even when the reason remains imperfectly clear.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds obsolete cables, a stopped watch, a broken pen, and other objects whose practical use has faded while their histories remain. It treats function as an incomplete measure of value, linking kept things to memory, deferred decisions, repair, consumer disposability, and aging. The comparison between broken objects and people makes the essay’s moral claim especially clear: usefulness should not determine whether something deserves care.

## Evidence line
> We are allowed to keep some things without a reason we can fully articulate.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a coherent, distinctive inquiry through recurring objects and a specific emotional conflict, rather than relying only on a generic thesis.
